utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in the proceedings. Novak Lukic and Tina Drolec today represent Mr. Perisic. Alex Fielding, our assistant, is with us. And Oonagh O'Connor, for the very first time, is our intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic. I would like us to discuss repair centres specifically. First of all, tell us, were you aware of what the system of these repair institutes was in the JNA, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina where they were located, and what did you know of them in general terms?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the system of the technical repairs institutes of the former Yugoslav People's Army. They remained where they were previously in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When the Army of Republika Srpska was established, these repairs institutes came under the direct command and competence of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already said as much yesterday. Did some of the repairs institutes that were previously located in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as part of the then-JNA, remain in the hands of the opposite sides, that's to say, outside of the remit of Republika Srpska and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was the repairs institute for communications devices in Travnik. It was taken by the Muslim Croat army and was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The repairs institutes which came under the chain of command of the VRS and were under the control of the Bosnian Serbs are the ones that I'm interested in, but can you tell us yourself which are the most important of these repairs institutes and what were their core activities in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important repairs institute was in Hadzici. This was due to its role of repairing combat vehicles as well as infantry and artillery weapons. It also modified these weapons. Another important repairs institute was Kosmos in Banja Luka. This was the only such institute which in the era of the former JNA repaired the assets for anti-aircraft combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us be quite precise on this issue. When you say that it was the only such institute, what was the relationship between this institute and subsequently the Army of Yugoslavia, if any?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another institute in Rajlovac which was equally important and which repaired plane engines for fighter planes that were part of the people's -- Yugoslav People's Army. It also catered for spare parts. It was the only repairs centre that had such a role in the whole of the Balkans, and it had some cutting-edge technology that could compete with that worldwide. Can you repeat, please, what your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was, if after the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was set up and the Army of Yugoslavia was set up there existed a relationship between that country and Kosmos, since you said that it was the only such institute, you also mentioned this other institute for plane bombs called Orao or Eagle, so what was their relationship with Yugoslavia, if any?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosmos repair centre in Banja Luka and the Orao or Eagle repair centre in Rajlovac, which was subsequently relocated, engaged in repairs of weapons and plane engines for the purposes of the Army of Yugoslavia. These were commercial jobs, commissioned, and they were the result of the business transactions between the federal Government of Yugoslavia and the Government of Republika Srpska. And there was direct co-operation between the Army of Yugoslavia, that's to say, between their repair centres, and the Army of Republika Srpska on the other hand, that's to say, the repair centres under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, do you know if these repairs institutes and the JNA did any sort of work for third countries; and, if so, what specifically?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Orao repairs institute back in 1990 had commissions for some 300 plane engines. They had been commissioned by Iraq and their army. These engines came to the Ora repairs centre in Rajlovac where they were repaired, and Iraq paid all its dues on this score with the directorate for weapons which was the so-called SDPR directorate in Belgrade. However, roughly 50 per cent of these engines were never sent back and stayed in the air repairs centre in Rajlovac, and this was due to international sanctions that had been imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You first mentioned the technical repairs institute in Hadzici. We heard evidence in this case that this institute had not been operational before the war. Can you tell us, to your knowledge throughout the conflict, was this repairs technical centre in Hadzici operational?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am fully familiar with the work of this institute. As of the 3rd or the 4th of May, 1992, through to the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Hadzici repairs institute was in the hands of the local authorities of the municipality of Hadzici. And the Serbs were in power then. So, in other words, it was in the hands of the Serbs. It was also under the control of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Hadzici, in other words, the Serb Territorial Defence structure in Hadzici. Then when the VRS came into being, this particular repairs institute was subordinated to or turned over to the Main Staff of the VRS and was immediately subordinated to the Main Staff of the VRS. The institute was operational throughout the war until the signing of the Dayton Accords at its location in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to look at a document now from the 65 ter Defence list which is 00843D. That's its 65 ter number. Can it be enlarged, primarily the B/C/S, and I'm interested in the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is titled "List of Territorial Maintenance Resources." And in the upper left-hand corner, it was signed by --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can it be, please, scrolled up so we can see the top left part of it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp and signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The signature is that of General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a list here of 32 legal personalities - I don't know how to call them - and it says "list of territorial maintenance resources," but the list does not include the repairs institutes you've just mentioned. Can you tell us what these entities are, companies or what they are, and what their role was in the -- in Republika Srpska in the area of repairs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were state-owned companies. Their core activities included the repairs of non-combat vehicles and non-combat assets such as communications devices and engineering devices as well as some other assets from the construction industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under 8 we have Cajevic Holding, which is probably on the next page in English. Can you tell us what the activity of this company was and how it fit into the repairs institute system?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rude Cajevic company from Banja Luka included several daughter companies and most of the plants manufactured communications devices. The former JNA used to purchase from this company a variety of communication devices that they used for the purposes of the JNA. The same holding manufactured certain parts for the automobile industry Crvena Zastava in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we receive an exhibit number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D402. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up document -- another 65 ter Defence list document, 00759D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a rather poor reproduction in terms of the fact that we can't see which republic is here -- is mentioned herein, but we can see that it was signed by Zarko Ljubojevic. So can you tell us, perhaps, which army this involved?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Colonel Zarko Ljubojevic who was in the technical department of the logistics sector of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The date on this document is August 1995, by which time you were no longer minister. Nevertheless, do you perhaps understand why they are addressing the Defence ministry here to obtain their approval in order to send these men to perform some steps in the Drina Corps? I do not wish to be leading you, but this abbreviation here, DK, that's the Drina Corps, isn't it, because I see that's what the English reflects as well; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about why it took addressing the defence ministry for this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact I do, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I had been replaced as defence minister and a new minister was appointed, Ninkovic, there were some open clashes between the defence ministry, the minister himself, and the Main Staff of the VRS, personified by General Ratko Mladic. Defence Minister Ninkovic unlawfully and wantonly issued an order removing all of the overhaul centres from the jurisdiction of the Main Staff of the VRS, resubordinating them instead to the defence ministry directly. For that reason, the request we are looking at was addressed to the defence ministry. Why? So that the defence minister himself could issue an authorisation for teams from these overhaul centres, as was their equipment, to be dispatched to the specified units of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a discrepancy here in the translation between the B/C/S and the English. The B/C/S original says that the group should be dispatched there because of "defektaze," whereas the English reads dive nose [as interpreted]. Witness, could you please explain what this word means, "defektaze"? I've never come across the word before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are simply defects affecting equipment and weapons. For example, the 90 millimetre self-propelled gun, the 130 millimetre gun, the 122 millimetre Howitzer, and so on and so forth. Guns, multiple rocket-launchers, you can see the list for yourself. They provide here a list of weapons and combat sets that were not being used because they were out of good working order. The teams being dispatched were supposed to perform something called "defektaze," which means disassembling these weapons and equipment in order to diagnose any defects. Batteries and spare parts would then be replaced to make sure that the weapons and equipment were now again in good working order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we please receive a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D403. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In very general terms, General, let us try and say a thing or two about the so-called special-purpose production industry, to be quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have another document from the Defence list, the 65 ter list, 01039D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we're waiting for the document to come up, General, you mentioned yesterday that a special-purpose industry was spread throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was, as a matter of fact, the case in the former Yugoslavia. I asked you something about the overhaul and maintenance centres. What about some of those production lines or the special-purpose production lines, did any of that end up in the hands of the second side and the third side, by which I mean not in the hands of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many of those special-purpose factories and production lines remained in their hands, including the artillery weapon factory of Bratstvo in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday. Any other ones?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Konjic ammunition factory which for the most part was a facility that was underground in the immediate vicinity of another underground facility that was meant in a state of emergency to house the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What type of ammunition was being produced in this facility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, the 2.7 millimetre machine-gun ammunition. But any kind of small arms ammunition could be produced there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just wait a minute, please. Whose hands did this facility end up in? Who now controlled it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both the Croats and the Muslims who controlled the town itself and the general Konjic area. There was another factory production facility at Bugojna producing hand-grenades, all types of mines and explosives. That factory as well was taken earlier on by the Croat-Muslim coalition and their army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please have a look at the document in front of you. This is a decision that have published in the Official Gazette of the VRS in June 1992. It specifies companies that will be producing weapons and military equipment, companies of special significance for the defence effort. There is a reference here, also, to the overhaul centres that you mentioned a while ago, and they appear to belong to the same group of companies based on this decision. Could you please tell us what were these companies that were producing weapons and equipment that, during the war, were in the hands of the authorities of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the companies stated in this decision. Pretis, Vogosca; Cajevac Holding, Banja Luka; Pobjeda, Gorazde; Hrasnica special vehicle production line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No need for you to go through the list.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but all of these companies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did these companies continue to operate throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. I'm sure, however, that Pobjeda Gorazde was not operational during the war because of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please shed more light on Articles 2 and 3 of this decision, if you can, sir. It's about the company manager being appointed. Can you tell us if that's really how it worked; were these managers appointed or replaced by the government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Article 3, talks about monitoring and supervision over these production lines, the ministry of the economy and the ministry of agriculture, is that how it worked in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, it worked like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did provide an example yesterday when you were talking about Pretis and the decision taken by General Mladic for him -- or, rather, the VRS, to call the shots on what happened with Pretis. Was that something that was done in concert with the ministry of the economy and agriculture or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an example of wanton and arbitrary action being taken by individuals, even if they were members of the army, and that was certainly not in keeping with this decision. This actually happened quite often, despite which it was impossible to prevent it. All those who made incursions of this kind would normally hold people at gun point while making their threats. My jurisdiction over the army or the -- specifically the Main Staff was not something that was formulated by any regulation or law. I had no power to issue any orders to the Main Staff of the VRS, nor indeed did I have any powers to stop occurrences such as these.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are referring to the period that you spent as a defence minister; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that this be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D404. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic now, the structure of the VRS itself. Who were the officers and NCOs of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS got its officers and NCOs from a number of different sources. The first of these being members of the former JNA who hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as those who remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina of their own free will. Their status-related issues were settled in Yugoslavia -- or, rather, through the VJ, although they remained members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting, sir, but I'd just like to go back to my original question to make sure we are being as specific as possible. You mean officers and NCOs of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that group alone and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second source was the -- those being educated at the military school centre in Belgrade. Normally on an annual basis there would be about 50 graduates who, upon completing the academy, would join the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How was their status regulated? Was their status like the status enjoyed by former JNA members or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had the same status as former JNA members. The next source, reserve officers and NCOs who were reserve officers and NCOs of the former JNA, remaining in the former JNA as officers and NCOs. And later moving on to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about their status, was it regulated in the same way as for the previous two categories, as far as the role of the FRY was concerned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, their status was only regulated within the VRS and the territory it covered. The next source, officers and NCOs being schooled and trained at the Rajko Balac Military School Centre in Banja Luka, which was directly under the Main Staff of the VRS. Following their training and education, officers and NCOs would normally receive certain ranks such as various NCO ranks, or, for example, the rank of second lieutenant, whereupon they would be dispatched to institutions and units of the VRS. Their status would normally be regulated within the VRS. This was something that was under the authority of the government and parliament of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've heard some figures being bandied about in this courtroom about the exact number of former JNA officers and NCOs, active-duty ones, now became members of the VRS. Given your position at the time, however, perhaps you could tell us more about the numbers concerning these others, former JNA reserve officers and NCOs whose status was regulated within Republika Srpska and the VRS in terms of percentage of figures, if you can, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to recall specific figures, but I think the number or percentage was slightly higher than that relating to the former JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll be showing you a document after the break in a bit to learn more about -- just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I will continue to call this group "former JNA reserve officers." Which ranks did they hold for the most part in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the law on the VRS that applied at the time, they could be promoted up to the rank of major. In exceptional cases, some men performing very high-ranking duties or establishment posts equivalent to the rank of lieutenant-colonel or colonel would be promoted nevertheless, regardless of the fact that they were part of the reserve component.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we have these names that we're using, active JNA and former reserve JNA; as far as the structure of the army itself in terms of how the men performed their duties, were there any difference in terms of powers and authorisations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no difference. They were all part of the same system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, I asked about ranks. What of the establishment posts that they were appointed to, up to what -- up to which establishment posts were these reserve officers appointed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the VRS was manned with officers and NCOs of the former JNA up to 20 per cent roughly. All the other establishment posts were filled by others, those who were financed by and whose status was settled within Republika Srpska and the VRS. For this reason, approximately 50 per cent of establishment posts of brigade commanders were filled with officers from the reserve force. These were, in other words, reserve officers of the former JNA who now became officers of the Army of Republika Srpska as was any other active-duty officer, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up another document from the 65 ter defence list, 01077D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I showed you this document during proofing, General. Can you please read it to yourself and then I'll ask for your comments.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us wait for the English translation to appear so that Their Honours can follow your testimony. This is an order from the Main Staff of the VRS dated the 7th of September, 1992, signed by the commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. Now, General, what was the reason behind this order? Why did Ratko Mladic issue this order?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this order because we brought it along when I was on the commission that I referred to yesterday which toured the units that were in the making. The objective of this order was to make sure that all the members of the VRS carried the VRS insignia. Those who refused to do so were discharged or released. The individuals or units which refused to do so were sent away from the VRS. There were officers who were self-proclaimed local commanders and who were not reserve officers of the JNA. They were ordinary soldiers. They were self-styled officers who, on their own initiative or with co-operation of local authorities, conferred upon themselves the ranks of most often captains or majors. We were forced to abolish these ranks and divest them of their powers and to issue documents banning the conferral of such ranks locally upon anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we receive an exhibit number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D405. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, have you heard of the 30th Personnel Centre, or had you heard of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be honest and say that I heard of the 30th Personnel Centre sometime in late 1994. I had certainly not heard of it in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, What did you hear of the 30th Personnel Centre? What was your information at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I had indicated that the 30th Personnel Centre kept records and personnel files relating to the status of the members of the former JNA who were members of the VRS and whose status was settled through that centre within the system of the Army of Yugoslavia pursuant to the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on the information you had, the 30th Personnel Centre was part of which army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The service that I was familiar with was housed in the personnel administration building of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to your new function.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we call up a 65 ter Defence document, 0049D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 00249D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, as we went through your CV, we made a passing reference to it. Can you tell us what this document is and how you came to be the minister of defence in the RS government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained it yesterday. Vladimir Lukic, prime minister designate, proposed that I be appointed defence minister. The Assembly of Republika Srpska elected the entire RS government, including myself as defence minister. Immediately thereafter, the president of the RS, Radovan Karadzic, issued a presidential decree appointing me to the establishment post of lieutenant-general since, by virtue of the establishment system, the post of the defence minister was the post of a lieutenant-general. Since it was an officer, a general, who occupied this post, I came under the system covering all the VRS generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, you continued receiving your salary as before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, if you know, who proposed that you be appointed to this post, and what was the relationship of other individuals holding positions to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not told who proposed me. A day before the Assembly of Republika Srpska went into session, the prime minister designate Lukic summoned me and told me that he was the one who nominated me for this position. President Karadzic was there as well. My reaction was that of exasperation because I wondered why nobody had consulted me previously. I was concerned that I would not be capable of discharging this function. Lukic's reply was that he had consulted a number of people, including General Mladic, who told him the following: We did not nominate Kovacevic, but we do agree that he be appointed to that position. A number of members of the SDS leadership, especially Velibor Ostojic, were opposed to my nomination as an officer of the former JNA and as a former commie that I should in fact occupy this post. And ultimately I agreed to be nominated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that they referred to you as a commie. What did they mean by it? Was it a derogatory term?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a derogatory term mocking all those who at one time used to be members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, at the time or at any point thereafter, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never been a member of any political party or any other organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question related to this document: Who was your predecessor in the position of defence minister and what became of him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was General Bogdan Subotic who, having been exposed to pressure from certain circles from the SDS party, was removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he hold any other position subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was advisor to the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, and he was also inspector within the office of the president of the republic who was charged with overseeing conduct within the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D406. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another document related to this issue, also from the 65 ter Defence list, 00251D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the document bears the same date as the earlier one, and it's also signed by Karadzic. Can you tell us what it is and why it was signed by President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a record of the hand-over of duty of the -- or, rather, the defence minister taking up his duty. I signed it, as did Radovan Karadzic in the capacity of the authority issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me let the witness finish his answer, but we were informed that this document and the previous document are not on the 65 ter list. I only -- sorry. We have not been notified that these were going to be exhibits. Now, I don't want to make a large issue out of this. It just makes it very inconvenient for us when we are managing this side of the bar table to deal with these exhibits because we haven't been informed that they were to be exhibits. I only make that observation. I don't object, and I don't object to the witness testifying about this. I can read it off of the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to respond, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I indicated to Mr. Harmon that I would be using -- and I'm just told by my Case Manager that we indicated it in the list under number 22 and under number 24, so the Prosecution was given notice of both documents. But more importantly, we also gave them notice of the document because we said that we would be using the personnel file of this witness which was also on the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under item 22 and 24, when was that notice given?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with us for a moment. We sent it on either Friday or Saturday. We will check this now. We sent two lists, since proofing lasted the whole weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, apparently they claim to have sent it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I am looking at a list with my Case Manager and those two items are not items 22 and 24 on the list, nor do I have, according to Ms. Javier, receipt of those two documents. So, again, I'm not -- don't care to make a large issue out of this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm just saying it makes it very difficult for us to manage this side of the case when we don't have the documents prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can understand. Now, it's your word against Mr. Lukic's. I'm not sure what to do about that, you know, because he claims to have sent it, you say you don't have it. I think the next best thing to do, Mr. Lukic, is to show us proof of delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Just a minute, Your Honours. Just a minute, please. We sent two lists separately. The personnel file document ... maybe it's best if we can inform you on this during the break. I can get the exact document from the list, if that's a problem for Mr. Harmon, but, personally, I believe that he should be familiar with this document because it's part of the personnel file. And it was on the OTP's 65 ter list. I do understand. I do understand. Just a minute, please. We are about to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar says he was copied on that e-mail. He has the document too. And the document on the screen is listed under item number 24. And apparently he received this document, this e-mail, on Friday -- yesterday. In the meantime, you can be finding your own proof of service, in case you believe you served it even earlier than yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not my intention to create any more confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to Mr. Registrar, it was not on the list of Friday, but it came in yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a list of yesterday. If there's a list that was sent yesterday, perhaps Mr. -- I see head shaking over there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we sent it yesterday. As Drolec has just explained, we sent this through to the Registry so that they might be better able to follow in e-court. That was for the Registry, but we sent a list to the OTP last weekend. That much is certain. And now we're trying to get that clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to proceed at this point with this document. Mr. Lukic and I can resolve this later. It's just -- as I say, it's not an objection to the witness testifying about this particular document, it's only the inconvenience I noted. And I'm prepared to proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I leave the matter to the parties to sort out during the break, please? And if there's any difficulty, then I would -- after the break, will ask you to show us proof of delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, why was it necessary to produce this order -- or, rather, this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was necessary to produce this document in order to regulate my service status such as my salary, salary bracket is what it says here, that also has further ramifications for my pension, social and health benefits, and so on and so forth. All of the contributions were paid out of this social benefits and so on and so forth. This was just to make sure that there was no interruption, not even a single day, to these payments being made, because this was the day I took up my duty. And there was a 15-, or 20-day gap, so to speak, for Subotic to leave and for me to come into office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we please receive a number for this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D407. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to discuss how the defence ministry was organised. General, as briefly as possible, and then we'll be looking at certain laws that tell us who had what powers.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took over as minister, the defence ministry had very low manning levels. It was poorly organised, and we were unable to re-organise straightaway and to make sure we were functioning in keeping with the law. I asked the government and the Main Staff to have a number of experts seconded to the ministry to help us along with our professional assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your request granted?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to a very small extent and never in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the best idea would be to look at the laws and see what the powers and authority were of your ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Defence Exhibit D108. Can we draw that one up, please. Thank you. It's page 2 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. Articles 10 and 13 of the Law on Defence are the paragraphs that we'll be looking at. We've just sent an e-mail ascertaining that the list was delivered on Saturday, 2.40 p.m., just to back up what I said previously. And I hope this resolves our misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand what you are saying. When you say "we have just sent an e-mail ascertaining that the list was delivered on Saturday," are you saying in the e-mail that you have sent that you have attached a copy of the e-mail that you sent on Saturday? Then say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You received it, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm checking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we have on our screens is the Law on Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please, of the B/C/S. And we have the right page in English already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The law is quite clear on this, and I'm not going to talk any -- about all these other things, the functions of the president of the republic and government, but what I'm looking at right now is Article 10, General, which talks about the powers of the defence ministry in terms of defence. General, read this to yourself, please, then I'll be asking you, Did the ministry really have the power that it says here and whether it took the steps that it was entitled to take under the Law on Defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of this is indeed prescribed. Nevertheless, in actual fact, Article 2, the Defence ministry was involved in assessing military and economic and other conditions. It was not the main implementing entity; rather, the Ministry of the Economy was. Number 3, the defence plan of the republic was never produced, nor did I have an opportunity to be involved in its drafting. Why? Because the leadership at the time wanted the Main Staff of the VRS to be in charge of the defence plan. Article 4, we did keep personnel records as those relating to equipment and materiel jointly with other ministries in terms of defining the organisation and tasks of the military administration during a state of emergency, and during my time as minister there was no defence inspection team in the Ministry of Defence. This was something that was done by General Subotic who was attached to the president of the republic and his cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please briefly go to Article 13 which is on the next page. It's a very short article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It talks about the work obligation or assignment. Look at Article 13, General, please. Are you aware of the fact that at the time during the war there was this thing called work obligation that was imposed and that applied throughout Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that was the case, and I was the person signing decisions in relation to all those subject to it, even as it related to ministers working in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to move on to a different law now, and I think this might be a convenient time for our break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record's clear, I stand corrected. We did receive notice of those documents. I apologise to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did you receive them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We received an e-mail on the 10th of July at 2.48 p.m. So I stand corrected. I apologise for the interruption. I apologise to counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome, sir. We take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to shed some light on the powers of the defence ministry but based on a different law, the law on the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the Prosecution Exhibit P191. I would like to know more about provisions in relation to Article 16. The B/C/S page reference is 26. In the English it's 38 and 39. Article 274, and then the articles that follow. 274, Article 274.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where it says "part 2," that heading. Thank you. I would like to comment on this provision that talks about the management of assets and materiel and financial transactions in the army. This is something that is familiar to you because you were defence minister and previously worked in the Main Staff. The law dates back to June 1992. General, I will not read this out loud. Once the Judges are done reading the first part of Article 274, maybe we can turn the page and move on to the next page. General, let me ask you first, based on Article 274, particularly paragraph 2 which defines assets, moveable and immovable property, property rights, and so on and so forth, to put it as simply as possible, would this include materiel and equipment as well as funds used to make sure the army is functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When it says "assets," it means funds which the RS government provides for in the budget. Funds are specially earmarked to be used by the VRS. Immovables, that means military facilities, installations, barracks, depots, petrol stations, and other structures and facilities used by the army. Moveable assets meaning weapons and all military equipment in the possession of the army. Ownership rights, what that means is the army was able to agree on certain contracts in terms of leasing and everything else that is employed under this term ownership rights or property rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on the following article, please, which talks about the army's funds. Can you read this article first, this one, and then we can pull it up and read Article 276 because the two are actually related. I think it might be beneficial for everyone to have both displayed on our screens. Just a minute, please, until we have that as well. The English specifically. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Military budget --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No need for you to read this out loud, General. My comment is, How is this -- how is this determined, who makes proposals, and who defines and approves the budget plan for the army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the VRS would draft a proposal or a draft plan of annual funding. This plan would include all of its needs in terms of the tasks that the VRS had to perform over a year. The draft proposal or the draft plan would be forwarded or submitted to the Ministry of Defence for analysis. The defence ministry would then assess the general circumstances which prevailed and would then go on to normally draft another proposal which would normally take into account about 30 per cent of the army's needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, I have a subsidiary question to ask here. When you say "take into account 30 per cent of the army's needs," why was that? Because you considered the army's demands to be too ambitious, or did you have a different reason to make amendments to the proposed budget drafted by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We made amendments to the plan based on fresh information regarding the situation concerning manning levels in the army's units. We determined that the demands were unrealistically high, enormous. That was why we made certain amendments and tried to present this within a more realistic framework. The modified plan was tabled to the RS government in the form of a proposal. The draft plan was then discussed and reviewed at a government meeting. When the proposal was discussed, normally members of the Main Staff were present, particularly General Djukic. They would accept this new plan at government meetings. Sometimes it was the case that the government accepted our plan, but sometimes the government had further amendments to make as a result of the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened next with the proposal once the government took its position on it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan would become part and parcel of the budget of Republika Srpska. As the funds came into the budget of Republika Srpska, the government would issue orders to -- or would instruct the finance minister to set aside certain funds and credit them directly to the account of the Main Staff of the VRS. It would also inform the defence ministry that this particular part of the budget, 5 or 10 per cent of it, dependent on what the amount was, had thus been executed, or this part of the budget was executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us stop here for a moment. At page 29, line 21, I would like us to clarify this bit. You mentioned the account of the Main Staff of the VRS. Did anyone have access to the account; and, if so, who did? Where was this account kept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The account through which the budget of the VRS was executed was located in a bank at Sokolac. Funds could be used from this account only when so instructed by individuals who had signatures certified with that bank, and this was General Tomic, assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, who was in charge of finances, budget, and accounting. I think that such deposited signatures were also held by General Milovanovic and General Mladic. Only these individuals from the Main Staff were able to dispose of these funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what way was the Ministry of Defence involved in this process or informed of the dispensing of these funds?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it came to this sort of funds that were earmarked in the budget for the army, it was the Main Staff which independently took decisions on the way in which these funds would be used. They were, however, duty-bound, and this is something that they did, to inform in writing the Ministry of Defence of the purposes for which these funds were spent. I myself received such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question which I don't think we cleared fully. Who gave the final green light for the budget of the RS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the government or the highest-ranking authority of Republika Srpska which had a final say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Assembly, that's to say, the parliament, have any involvement in the adoption of the budget?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A budget that was in this way formulated and adopted would be the subject of discussion at one of the sessions of the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this for us: Article 276, in part where it says "regular work and regular operations and maintenance," what does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are funds earmarked for general purposes, for overhead expenses such as electricity, et cetera, public utilities, salaries, pension and social benefits of all members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would the salaries of those officers referred to earlier on who previously belonged to the reserve force of the JNA also be paid out from this budget line?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant when I said that this particular line would cover the salaries of the members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about these materiel supplies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an item which relates to the funds used for the purchasing of weapons, ammunition, and other materiel and technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In item 5, military pensions are mentioned. Can you tell us who received their pensions from the RS budget?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not privy to this issue at all. I think that -- or I can say for at that fact that, at the time, the Ministry of Defence did not set aside funds for anyone's pensions. I suppose that this part of the budget of the Ministry of Defence was used to pay amounts into the pension fund of Republika Srpska which were to serve as contributions for those members of the VRS that received their salaries from the RS government. I suppose that out of this fund pensions were paid, then, to those pensioners who had gone into retirement at the time of the SFRY, or at the time of the JNA in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Article 294, which is on the following page, I think, for both the B/C/S -- or, rather, it's page 41 in English. Article 294, which is at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and continues on the following page. The very bottom on the right-hand side. There. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you finish reading, we will turn to the following page to complete the reading of the article. I'm interested in paragraph 3 above all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn the page for both versions. And in the B/C/S can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this particular paragraph which starts with "Officers in units and institutions shall act ..." et cetera. What you said a moment ago, General, about the various funds at their disposal, is this regulated by this part of the law?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The funds belonging to the RS government could be used by the Main Staff, that's to say, the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, Ratko Mladic, and by the minister of defence as a member of the RS government, in part, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which part of the funds were you entitled to dispose of as minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would dispose of those funds for which I had the appropriate authorisation from the government. The government would credit those funds to the account of the Ministry of Defence, and I was able to dispose of the funds to procure assets required by the VRS in keeping with the budget plan or pursuant -- or, rather, in keeping with the special decision issued by the president of the republic, by the government, or the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've finished with this document. We'll get back to the issue of the budget and the extent to which, in fact, the budget featured within the finances of the army. Let's go back to the ministries. Which other ministries -- or let me be more precise. Did the finance ministry in any way participate in the implementation of these laws and in the activities of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Often times at the request of General Mladic and most often at the request of General Djukic, the president of the republic or the prime minister would issue orders to the finance minister, without the involvement of the Ministry of Defence, to transfer funds in a certain amount in dinars or foreign currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the Ministry of Commerce have any role to play in the finances of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever fuel or any other goods were being procured such as foodstuffs, medications, any goods of general consumption, or anything that did not involve combat-related goods, these sort of procurements would fall within the competence of the Ministry of Commerce. In such cases, the government would adopt conclusions where a part of the funds from the budget of the Ministry of Defence and the army would be transferred to the Ministry of Commerce, which would use the funds to procure these goods. And as I said, most often it was fuel, foodstuffs, and any other goods of general consumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the directorate for commodity reserves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of that directorate for commodity reserves, because the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had issued a decree whereby all the reserves of the former Yugoslavia present in the territory of Republika Srpska or throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina were transferred to the competence of the Government of Republika Srpska and the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in early 1992 or in mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What became of the fuel reserves that were present in the BH and which had previously belonged to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the fuel reserves of the former Yugoslav People's Army and of the former Supreme Command of the SFRY, as well as the reserves of the SFRY which were referred to at the time as the federal reserves, were placed under the control and competence of the commodity reserves of Republika Srpska. Or when it came to the other part of the territory under the control of the Croats and Muslims, it was placed within the competence of their authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the commodity reserves that were placed within the competence of the RS, who had the direct authority to decide on the way in which these reserves would be disposed of? And I'm primarily interested in fuel.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the regulation, it was only the government that could do that and possibly the parliament. Exceptionally, the president of the republic as the supreme commander could also dispose of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's another ministry that I'm interested. If you can explain what role it played in the functioning of the defence system and what links, if any, it had with the VRS; I'm talking about the industry ministry. And what did that ministry have to do with all these topics that we've been covering?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The industry ministry or Ministry of Industry comprised special-purpose production companies. Normally, there were some government decisions telling them to create conditions for production in those companies of those products that were required for defending Republika Srpska, primarily for the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How often did the government meet, and what shape did the meetings take? I'm talking about your time as minister.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally on a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any extraneous persons attending those government meetings who were not members of the government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the Main Staff of the VRS would be called on a regular basis, as well as the managers of all important companies, especially those that dealt with commodity reserves. There were representatives there of other state institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the first assignments that you were given in your capacity as minister, following your appointment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first assignment that the defence ministry got - and that means that I got in my capacity as minister - was the conclusion of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, that the ministry should start re-organising and restructuring the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you embark on that assignment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took a particularly conscientious, serious, and thorough approach in terms of tackling that assignment. The first thing I did was to conduct consultations with experts in those fields. I also consulted some people from UNPROFOR and other foreigners. I tried to elicit from them their experiences on how to create a modern and efficient army. I also went through a large body of literature describing the structure of various European armies, especially those who are NATO members. Two or three months later, I completed a new chart for a re-organisation and formation of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the briefest of terms, what was the gist of this re-organisation effort?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist was for the VRS to be reduced in terms of manpower. It was to number 150.000 soldiers and officers at the very most. Nevertheless, it was supposed to become a disciplined army, a rigorously organised army where discipline reigned and rules of conduct were observed. One had to know at each point in time who was responsible for what and who was issuing orders in relation to what. About 80.000 members who were still members of the army should leave the army's ranks and go to the industry sector so that the other companies, such as agricultural ones, could continue their production to benefit the people, the army, and cater to all the needs of the VRS itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this proposal accepted?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first showed this proposal to the RS government. The government backed my proposal with no reservation whatsoever. There wasn't a single vote against the proposal. Nevertheless, the government proposed that the Supreme Command, too, should address this issue. There was a meeting of the Supreme Command at which the proposal was fully endorsed. Nevertheless, the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, refused to sign the document, this re-organisation chart, until members of the Main Staff of the VRS were given a chance to address the issue at the following meeting of the Supreme Command. This meeting, too, was then held, and people from the Main Staff were there. I'm certain that General Milovanovic was present. I again presented the plan. Nevertheless, the representatives of the Main Staff flat out rejected the plan, advising the president of the republic to by no means sign the plan. Needless to say, the plan was never implemented. But I was now facing a difficult situation, because the army never trusted me. On the other hand, the SDS did not trust me either. I've often found myself entertaining thoughts of resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can try to be more specific about this. You told us that your appointment as minister came in January and then it took a couple of months. Can you tell us, roughly speaking, when this debate took place at the Supreme Command meeting when the representatives of the Main Staff opposed your proposal? That was in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it went on all the way up to the end of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the arguments that people from the Main Staff put forward?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember some of their arguments. General Milovanovic said, Mr. President, if your horse is strong and working well, you don't need a new one. The VRS is performing its tasks perfectly well. There is no need to introduce any changes to the existing system it. The other thing was they refused to have any cuts in terms of manpower, and they refused to deal with the issue of local authority interference with the command and control system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We shall now discuss the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter Defence document 00960D. 00960D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a decision to establish the Supreme Command of the Army of Republika Srpska. The date is the 30th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull this up slightly. I'm not sure if our own copy reflects the signature, who signed it, or, for that matter, if the English does. Yes, thank you. Yes. I just felt that had to be checked. The B/C/S is hardly legible; nevertheless, the translators were successful in deciphering this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, the decision speaks for itself. How was the Supreme Command established, and who made up the Supreme Command? Articles 1 and 2 address this issue. Let me first ask you this: Were you involved in the work of -- as we heard from your previous answer but just to be quite specific, were you involved in the work of this body?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in the work of the Supreme Command in my capacity as defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How were the dates determined when the Supreme Command meetings were held, or were they held on an ad hoc basis?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings took place whenever circumstances so dictated. We never set any particular dates for these meetings. The meetings were always set by the president of the republic and supreme commander Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 5 of this decision talks about the final decision of the Supreme Command of the VRS, and this is something that is within the remit of the president of Republika Srpska. Can you please interpret for us how this panned out in purely practical terms. What would a debate as one of these meetings look like, and who would take the final decision?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All members of the Supreme Command, as well as those invited to attend meetings of the Supreme Command without necessarily being members, had the right to discuss any topics on the agenda. They had the right to discuss and make their own proposals. Nevertheless, only the president of the republic, who was also the supreme commander, had the power to overrule any of these proposals, to accept the proposals, or perhaps adopt an altogether different solution. None of the Supreme Command members, and that really means no one at all, had the power to take decisions regarding any of the issues debated at a Supreme Command meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. What I would like to ask you now is, What topics exactly were debated or discussed at the Supreme Command meetings for as long as you were there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally problems regarding the establishment of the army, problems regarding military supplies, the organisational and establishment structure of the army, the army's assignments and the way the army was used, especially as it related to large-scale combat operations. Negotiations with the international community, negotiations with UNPROFOR, regulations that were to be adopted by the parliament, and other issues too. Most of the topics related to the defence effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not be dealing with these issues specifically. We may touch upon them later on. But can you tell me, Was there a debate on military operations of the VRS, and were decisions taken about the VRS military operations at these meetings of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no. Operations were planned outside the knowledge of the members of the Supreme Command and government. The operations lay solely within the competence of the Main Staff, with the knowledge and approval of the president of the republic. The meetings of the Supreme Command discussed the request put forward by the Main Staff of the VRS which were for the most part put forward by General Mladic and which discussed what it was that the government was supposed to provide the VRS with in order for the operations to be carried out. Operations had code-names such as the Sava, the Drava, the Drina, et cetera, and we had no idea what part of the territory these operations referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Sava, the Drava, the Drina," I suppose you use these names as an example?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does not necessarily follow that any of these titles was, in fact, used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Supreme Command meetings discuss any of the VRS directives?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Normally, based on the debate, the president of the republic would issue orders and directives on all the issues the discussion touched upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in one of the topics that were the subject of the discussions at these Supreme Command meetings. At page 42, line 7, you mention negotiations with the international community. Were you informed at Supreme Command meetings, and were discussions taking place about the peace initiatives and proposals for the resolution of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Supreme Command was reported to and informed on the various proposals for cease-fires and peace agreements. One other question that was discussed was the humanitarian aid convoys and their release into the protective enclaves of Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa on the part of the VRS. Also discussed were issued related to negotiations, which I was involved in on one occasion with General Morillon, and it had to do with the shelling of Sarajevo. Also discussed were negotiations and talks with other individuals, especially UNPROFOR commanders, and they had to do with Gorazde, with those enclaves, and with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I forget, Your Honours, can I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D408. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I want to touch upon a topic that has to do with what we've just discussed, and I would like to spend some more time on this issue. Did the Supreme Command discuss the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan of 1993 regarding the resolution of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This issue was not discussed because this was not within the purview of the Supreme Command. However, what did take place was a free discussion of the proposal itself, more as a way of assisting the president in his decision by discussing the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was your position as minister of defence in relation to the Vance Plan at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in the matter in any way, but I had a right to voice my opinion and discuss the matter just as everyone else did. The commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic, played a decisive role in the defence system on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if an agreement was reached in Greece in Solun, did President Karadzic have anything to do with it, and what was the reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed at the meeting of the Supreme Command that the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, had placed his initials on an agreement in Athens. The People's Assembly of Republika Srpska was supposed to speak its mind on this agreement, and the only binding decision would be the one carried by the Assembly itself, as far as this issue was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the People's Assembly meet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. At Jahorina at Rajska Dolina Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you if you attended this meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was officially invited by the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska to attend this session, and I was there in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the date or an approximation of it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in early May. At any rate, it was in May. I don't know the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it was the 5th of May, 1993, the 13th Session. I don't think my learned friend will mind me saying this. I will not ask for the minutes from the meeting to be admitted into evidence. Can you tell us, just before the session was opened, what was the general sentiment on the part of the deputies with regard to the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular proposal which was initialed by the president of the republic Radovan Karadzic was discussed not only by the Supreme Command but also by the government, and I took part in those discussions. Both the Supreme Command and the government decided that only the deputies of the Republika Srpska parliament could decide on the matter and that everybody would accept their decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any particular guests present at this meeting, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There were extraneous guests there. I remember that because I was part of the reception party charged with receiving these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who do you remember arriving at the Assembly meeting among the extraneous guests?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally saw and shook hands with the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Dobrica Cosic; president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic; Momir Bulatovic; Greek prime minister Michas Takis; and other dignitaries who did not attend this part of the session when President Karadzic reported to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened in this part of the session where the RS leadership was present and these -- this part of the leadership?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, five or six of us who were the core leadership of Republika Srpska - and I was next to the prime minister - once we greeted everyone, we stepped into a room -- or, rather, we stepped into the hall where the Assembly meeting was to take place, refreshments were served, coffee and drinks. These were just preliminary discussions, and people were supposed to refresh themselves. At one point, President Slobodan Milosevic asked the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, the following: Mr. President, have you prepared your deputies in order to make sure that the plan is accepted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK'S REPLY WAS
