utterances.text: Mr. President, we did not prepare anyone, including the deputies of our Assembly. We did not exert any sort of influence on them either to accept or reject the proposal. Everyone has been given their own personal freedom and discretion to decide based on their conscience. Milosevic said: Very well then, the only thing we want to avoid is for something nonsensical to happen in the end, just so that something silly would not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you understand what the representatives of the FRY said, that something silly should not happen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, their position was that they wanted the proposal to be accepted at any cost and they were there to lobby for it. However, Milosevic was unhappy with the response he got from the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, the response that he gave him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we have the minutes from this session here in this case. We will not be discussing it at length. Just tell us what sort of decision was taken in the end, and who took the floor? Did you yourself take the floor in the debate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said that I would accept any decision, both as a minister and as a human being, taken by the deputies of this Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic address the Assembly; and, if so, do you recall what his position was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the deputies took part in the debate, and most of them were against the adoption of the plan. The ministers on -- of the government, including myself, didn't have a decision-making power in this, so we did not get involved. General Mladic discussed at length the consequences that the adoption of this plan would have, and he said that the plan was not good at all and that it had to be rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did the deputies -- or, rather, did the guests address the Assembly and take part in the debate, and what did they say?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the guests took the floor, and some of them addressed the Assembly on more than one occasion. They all were in favour of the adoption of the plan because they wanted the war to end and they wanted the sanctions to be lifted from Yugoslavia. Some of them addressed the Assembly of Republika Srpska in pleading tones in order to try and urge them to accept the proposal. The Greek prime minister Michas Takis also addressed the Assembly, and he also pleaded with the deputies to adopt the plan. At the interval, he wanted to talk to me and asked me to provide him with some figures and information. He urged me to take the floor and urge the deputies to accept the plan. I told him in reply that I was not a deputy and did not have the power of getting involved in the debate in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. What was the ultimate decision? Was the vote secret or public?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Votes were cast, and most of them were against the plan. A number of deputies were abstained -- abstained, and I don't recall that anyone was against.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that anyone was in favour of the adoption of the plan?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do not recall any of the deputies voting in favour of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there anything that remained etched in your memory from this particular session? What was the reaction on the part of the guests?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Base on the established protocol, there were members of the MUP of Serbia represented there as well. We decided again to organise a formal sendoff of the guests in the way envisaged by the protocol. As I was heading toward the exit within the party of guests and deputies, I heard such vulgar expletives both from Milosevic, Bulatovic, and Cosic, and everyone there as left me speechless. I just could not imagine such dignitaries uttering oaths of that kind. They refused to formally greet anyone there. They practically fled the building, got into their cars; and it was only the police who managed to catch up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked that we move into private session because I would like to discuss with the witness two entries from the documentation that were referred to as Mladic's notebooks. First of all, I should like to apply for your leave to be given 65 ter 0337D, to actually -- to include them on the list. And for Mr. Harmon, this is folder 36/1; that's where the entry comes from. And the date of the entry is 17 and 19 June, 1993. I can also provide ERN numbers for Mr. Harmon, but I'm sure that he will be able to find it easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have two different translations in English, could we have the first translation on our screens. And the pages in the B/C/S and English are the same. This is the B/C/S. That's right. And then the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we can tell, the date is the 17th of June, 1993. Chronologically, we are picking up where we left off in the previous document. It says "meeting with defence minister." General, during our proofing, I showed you this document and we discussed it. Based on that, do you remember meeting General Mladic in June, and do you remember discussing what is specified here in this entry? Perhaps you want it read back to you. I'm not sure if you can read the Cyrillic text. Number 1: Establishing the ministry and organising the ministry.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this is accurate. I asked General Mladic on several occasions to have a number of officers who were experts seconded to me to help me out with the field of military industry, specifically, and with finances. I wanted to have those officers seconded by the army to the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was General Mladic's position on this issue, on VRS officers working for the ministry? Did he back your proposals?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but he had a tough time making the actual decisions in terms of renouncing on the assistance of such qualified officers. He wasn't willing to let them go and believed their services were more necessary for the army than for the ministry. Nevertheless, he did second a number of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of the civilian authorities vis-à-vis this issue? The ministry being reinforced, if you will, by people from the army. You talked about the position of certain politicians, but what was the general position that prevailed in terms of the army being involved in the ministry's work in this way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS who were in power opposed this possibility of having officers work for the ministry, particularly JNA officers. They always opposed this. It was a considerable difficulty that I had to deal with. I was supposed to set up a ministry that would have qualified people working there, which would enable us to discharge our tasks in a professional way and in keeping with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move on to the next page. I have a brief question about the substance there. Could he have the English too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Towards the top of the page, we can see you state: "To begin with, I would need Colonel Malcic, Zujic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Dubovac seconded." Do you remember asking for these men specifically?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Colonel Malcic was a personnel and HR expert. Zujic was an expert in the quartermasters duties. And Dubovac was an expert in finance and budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we move on to the following entry immediately, the following meeting and talk about that. It is described here as the Supreme Command of the VRS meeting. The 23rd of June 1993 is the date reflected there. Who seems to be in attendance? Some of these men, I understand why they were there, but this man named Adzic, the last person mentioned here, who might that be?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the minister of the interior in the RS government. Before that, he used to work as president of Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, if I may ask you one thing, you're listed here as one of the attendees, and there's an entry that reflects one of your own contributions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much longer are you going to be on this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we'd best simply stop now. I reckoned I had another 10 minutes, but I was wrong, Your Honour. Maybe we just best move back into open session. I might spend some time on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to announce the presence of Monsieur Laurent Vuillemin who is a Case Manager on our team and who will be attending this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You are welcome. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back into private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, first of all, what it says here, I'm not sure if you're able to read it, Mr. Karadzic's contribution, it reads: "Based on our assessment and the assessment of the rest of the world, we have won and will be given a state. Both the Croats and we should do something so that the Muslims get some territory in central Bosnia. First there was talk about 38, then 33 municipalities, and now we are talking about the treasures of Bosnia in 30 municipalities. America must find someone to blame (Germany) to change their policy." In relation to what we discussed a while ago about the 13th Assembly session at Jahorina and the decision that was taken, what was the political reality that you faced in Republika Srpska, given the fact that the Vance-Owen Plan had been rejected? And a month after that discussion we see President Karadzic saying this. How did he get the information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no specific information myself. I do believe, however, that Karadzic actually uttered these words at the Supreme Command meeting. This was firsthand information, if I can put it that way. I know that after the proposal had been rejected at the Assembly meeting, Karadzic was involved in intense talks with all the international players in an attempt to find a way out of the crisis and possibly find a peaceful solution, a solution that would leave the three peoples involved equally happy without any victors and without the vanquished. This was Karadzic's general position which he held as early on as the very outset, back in 1992, when demands were made to draw borders to separate the Serbs from the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In a general sense, what Karadzic was saying here, was that common place for members of the Supreme Command to be informed about information such as this and about his position regarding the peace talks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, but this wasn't something that happened all the time, but it was customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two pages further into the document, same entry, same meeting, but I would like you to comment on a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right there, we can stop there, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have a comment from you. What it says about Krajisnik. And then it reads, all -- I can't read this word, even though it's in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we zoom in to the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads, "personal and arrogant and self-sufficient." General, in your opinion, are these words actually uttered by Mr. Krajisnik, or is it just an addendum?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we see, if you look at this entry, normally these are quotes, someone is saying something. But the way it's written here, how does this strike you? Do you perhaps remember what was said? Is this something that Mr. Krajisnik actually said, or is this about something else? "Everything directed and subordinated to" - I'm not sure what it says - are personal, arrogant, self-sufficient. What could that possibly mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajisnik might have been talking about Mladic, making an assessment of Mladic being like that. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object. This witness apparently doesn't have personal knowledge about this quotation. He is speculating and therefore his testimony is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree. I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, just what you remember. I have here a suggestion by my client. Mr. Perisic claims that this word is mentioned again in a different line "Zabrdje," therefore I'm re-reading this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you reading what Mr. Perisic is saying here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say you have here a suggestion by your client, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Perisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But Mr. Perisic has not taken the stand yet to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but he's making a suggestion on how I should phrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Phrase your question without referring to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, if we read the Cyrillic script here, everything directed and subordinated to his "Zabrdje." What does that mean to you, "Zabrdje."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zabrdje is a village in which Momcilo Krajisnik was born. It is on the outskirts of Sarajevo in the Rajlovac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Your Honours, there is a discrepancy between my reading of the B/C/S and the translation that we see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed that's what's giving -- causing me problems, because I don't see "everything." I don't see the word "everything;" I see "channelled."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it out loud, and I'll ask the interpreters in the booths to confirm whether my reading of the Cyrillic is correct the way I see it. "Krajisnik: Everything directed and subordinated to his Zabrdje. Personal and arrogant and self-sufficient."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what does "Zabrdje" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just asked the General, and he explained in the previous answer. Page 56, line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, the word "Zabrdje," what is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this, and I'll repeat it. Momcilo Krajisnik was born in the village of Zabrdje, the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. That's his native village. Mladic is making an assessment here at this meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object again, Your Honours. It calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not Mladic speaking here; it's supposed to be Krajisnik. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have my own theory. I think the more Mr. Harmon reads these documents, he will tend to agree with me more and more. Personal points of view of the author are often given here or stated. That is my theory, my position. I understand Mr. Harmon, and we shall not be asking the witness to speculate. So if the witness is unable to help us, we'll probably be unable to elicit an answer from him. But I thought this might be a good way to familiarise ourselves with something that we shall be encountering further into the document. I will drop the line of questioning, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next entry reads "Lukic." Who was Lukic at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the RS government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Next page, please. What exactly is he recorded as saying there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the next page in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The entry reads as follows: "Some battalions have three or four suppliers. Number of officers are busy doing anything rather than dealing with the front line." What was the meaning of Mr. Lukic's words in this particular entry?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information is accurate. The president of the RS government Lukic obtained this information normally by touring units in my presence. We shared the view that this was not a good thing and that the supreme commander should do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further down, there's an entry which reads: "A number of commanding officers and authorities provide very imprecise details." Who provides information, and what sort of information is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that from the very outset local commanders had their own local sponsors and most often these were municipalities, private businessmen, and state-owned companies whose managers were members of the SDS. They provided all the necessary supplies to the local brigade without informing the superior command of the corps, and the corps in turn did not have any information to report on to the Main Staff. Accordingly, the Main Staff was not provided precise information as to the quantities of combat assets available to these units. This was general practice at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, and can it be placed under seal for the time being. And I would also like to ask to move into open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And may it please be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to a new topic, that's to say, supplies of materiel and technical equipment in the VRS during your term of office as minister of defence. I would also like to hear whatever knowledge you might have on this issue which dated from the previous period. Based on the information privy to you, what was the level of equipment that the VRS had and were the supplies of weapons it received sufficient?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was sufficiently equipped with all types of weapons which had been at the disposal of the then-JNA -- or, rather, the then-former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how well were the other two participants in the conflict, the BH army and the HVO, equipped with weapons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on intelligence and other types of information I received on a daily basis, I knew that the Croatian Defence Council was well armed with weapons it received from the Republic of Croatia. I knew that the Muslim side, that's to say the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was comparatively poorly equipped but that it had been receiving all manner of weapons from abroad. The weapons were transported by planes landing in the Dubrava airfield in Tuzla. I also knew what types of weapons and in what quantities were provided in individual planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in the subsequent years of the conflict, did the supplies of weapons held by the HVO and BH increase or decrease in time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the HVO was concerned, the numbers stagnated, but the BH army received increasingly large amounts of weapons and ammunition. Furthermore, fighters were joining the BH army from Arab countries, they were referred to as al-Qaeda, and they posed a large threat to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now discuss ammunition. What sort of ammunition supplies did the VRS have at the beginning of the war, and did that situation change subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war and through to the end of 1993, the VRS had sufficient quantities of ammunition and fuel. Objectively and realistically speaking, there was no need for certain types of ammunition to be additionally obtained because the quantities were sufficient. There were only a couple of types of ammunition that were in short supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the subsequent period from late 1993 onwards, what was the situation with regard to ammunition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the start of 1994, the problem of shortage of ammunition and fuel became gradually more prominent. This was a problem that I personally and the members of the Main Staff were confronted with because we received requests for ammunition. I believed the requests to be exaggerated and unrealistic. Such quantities of ammunition were neither necessary nor was it easy to obtain them in such quantities at such short notice. I normally instructed them to go to apply to their local brigades and to inspect the weapons depots they had, but they would see that they had ammunition in enough -- in sufficient quantities which could be used in a rational manner, rather than applied to the state to use its resources to obtain ammunition that was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will be focusing on fuel later on; that's why I wanted us to discuss ammunition first. In what way was ammunition procured for the needs of the VRS in the period we are discussing now which is from 1994 onwards?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the standard procedure. The army or the Main Staff would state their needs to the Ministry of Defence or directly to the supreme commander. And if they addressed the commander, then they would normally at the same time inform the prime minister and myself. The government and the Supreme Command were responsible for seeing what sort of ammunitions were required and in what quantities. The ammunition was obtained from local manufacture in the weapons factories in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then also from the special-purpose industry companies in the FRY. Whereas for those types of ammunition which could not be obtained from these sources, the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic, would always tell us that he would go and see Slobodan Milosevic in order to try and resolve the matter. Normally, on his return, which would be 10, 15, or 20 days later, he would inform either the Supreme Command or the inner circle of the government and certain members of the Main Staff that president Slobodan Milosevic had promised him that the Army of Yugoslavia would provide the ammunition or that he, through the Supreme Defence Council, and sometimes he personally, would see to it that the matter is resolved. And it was personally General Mladic who was given the authority to resolve such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During such meetings did President Karadzic tell you what General Perisic's position was on the issue of the Army of Yugoslavia providing supplies and materiel and technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he did so often. I remember that once Karadzic literally said the following: General Perisic will not give ammunition out of his own reserves because that would undermine the reserves of the Army of Yugoslavia; or, General Perisic will not allow for ammunition to be provided from Krusik Valjevo or in other locations where ammunition was being manufactured for the needs of the Army of Yugoslavia. So whenever there was a quantity of weapons that had been ordered by the Army of Yugoslavia for their needs, he would not allow for these assets to be set aside for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said at page 62, line 10, that Karadzic said that General Perisic stated that if such reserves were provided, that would undermine the combat readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would undermine the prescribed quantity of combat sets that had been earmarked for the Army of Yugoslavia, which automatically meant that it would threaten the combat readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already discussed this issue, but we are dealing with the period from 1994 onwards now. This system of providing supplies to local units from local sources, how did it work, and who would be involved in the process of providing the army with supplies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially in the period following the imposition of sanctions on Yugoslavia, the supplying of the VRS with ammunition with the involvement of local authorities and local units was used increasingly. They also relied on sponsors. Normally this would be carried out without the knowledge of the Ministry of Defence, especially without the knowledge of the government, and sometimes even without the knowledge of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to elicit comments from the witness on a number of Prosecution documents on these issues. Can we first call up P1259, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the order of General Ratko Mladic dated the 24th of October, 1993. General, I am interested in the first part of the document. And can you tell us, Were you aware of what is stated here and what prompted General Mladic to issue an order with such strict instructions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason that I'm familiar with behind such an order from Ratko Mladic is the request that I put forward at the meeting of the Supreme Command and the request put forward by the prime minister as well as by other members of the Supreme Command. As a result, the supreme commander President Karadzic issued an order instructing General Mladic to issue such an order which would be distributed to all the subordinate units with a view to introducing order into the system of procurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have information, as is stated in this order, that some of the materiel and technical equipment ended up in the hands of the enemy, as is said here, and led to certain individuals making an enormous amount of money for themselves? Do you know what the author meant by this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this issue. This was one of the painful issues to me as an individual and a professional. I could not accept in any way that members of the VRS locally, as well as sponsors, should be selling weapons and ammunition to the opposite side. This was an occurrence that was lethal to the VRS in which nobody wanted genuinely to dispense with. And it was very detrimental. There are individuals who are still wealthy thanks to the activities dating from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up P1247, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document produced by General Djukic delivered to all units. He invokes a response that came from the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ. Sir, were you familiar with General Perisic's position regarding the way the supplies came and went from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in communication with General Perisic, but I got to learn his position at Supreme Command meetings, normally through Karadzic or through Mladic -- or, rather, only through Karadzic and Mladic. I cannot, myself, speak to this because I haven't read it. Nevertheless, as far as the Supreme Command meetings are concerned, as I said, I heard that Perisic was trying to put a stop to this arbitrary waste and in expenditure of army reserves at a local level as well as everywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second sentence reads: "This way of addressing is surprising, and it is especially inconceivable that this process is brokered by some commanders and commands of VJ units." Djukic quotes Perisic as saying that. Did you have any information indicating that this kind of meddling was involved?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learned that both from General Djukic and at Supreme Command meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the next document. It's very much like this one. This is P1802.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I find this document interesting because of the date, July 1995. That's two years after the earlier document. Midway down the page: "The commands from the corps level down, contrary to warnings and their attention being drawn to the damage caused" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel please read this again slowly and provide a reference on where we can find this in the actual document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking that could you please read this again and provide a reference so that they could know where you are reading from. And read slowly. And could we scroll up, please. We don't see anything in the English here except the heading really. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the English portion that is relevant for my purposes is actually on the next page, Your Honours, what I'm reading from. Yes, it's right there at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Certain commands from corps level down, contrary to warnings and instructions about the damaging effect, have continued with the practice of contacting directly, without authorisation, state organs, institutions, companies, humanitarian organisations, and societies, and individuals in the FRY, on behalf of the VRS," et cetera. My question: General, did you know that the practice, as described in previous documents, continued? When I say "practice," I mean ammunition was obtained but not at the level that was prescribed by previous documents, and, generally speaking, equipment in the FRY.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the practice. I've answered this question on two occasions already, saying that this practice and similar practices continued throughout the war. I also said that this practice was particularly intensive after sanctions had been imposed against the FRY. The practice continued all the way up to the Dayton Peace Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about VRS units, were they in a position to themselves procure or purchase ammunition from special-purpose production lines and factories in the FRY? Could they do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was receiving information indicating that local authorities and local units from municipalities and donors from Republika Srpska were able to purchase ammunition in a special-purpose production factories across the FRY. And they were also able to take all their purchases back to units, normally those of brigade or battalion level within the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at P1234, an OTP document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we see here is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps. If we turn to page 3, we'll see that it was signed by chief of the technical services, Colonel Dragoljub Jankovic. Nevertheless, what I want to be looking at is page 1. He was chief of the technical administration; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was chief of the technical services in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake. That's right. We see that this is, if I may call it that, a report under sources from which different kinds of ammunition came to the 1st Krajina Corps. The period is the 1st of January through the end of September 1994. I would like to focus on entry number 4. Bullet 7.62.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you, Mr. Lukic. I'm just asking that we zoom in on the English, please, at number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in the B/C/S for my benefit too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll need to move the document to the right in order to be able to follow what I'm reading and so that I can have your comments, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, 7.62 bullet: What weapon is that, and how essential is this to the functioning of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entry number 4 reads: 7.62 millimetre bullet AP, means automatic rifle, Kalashnikov specifically, and PAP [as interpreted], meaning semi-automatic rifle. Again, the calibre is 7.62. That covered almost 99 per cent of the weapons carried by actual soldiers and members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. We have this column - if we can move the English - that reads, "Logistics Bases of the Main Staff." The figure there is 7.352.000. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps, following orders and dispositions, received or took delivery in these logistics bases of the VRS Main Staff a total of 7 billion 352 thousand bullets -- 7 million 352 thousand bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next column is empty. It reads, "Received from the RS." And then next one reads, "Received from the FRY." 9.998.000 bullets. Who in the FRY produced this ammunition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special-purpose factory known as Prvi Partizan. It was based in the town of Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under the regulations of the FRY, do you know under whose authority this special-purpose production actually was in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were state-owned companies. Their military production programme, special-purpose production, was under the defence ministry of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are done with this document. Thank you. I think this document will be easier to analyse later on, having done this. As far as this type of ammunition is concerned. Next document, another OTP document -- or, rather, my mistake. This is a 65 ter list document, a Defence document, 65 ter 02048D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have a close look slowly, General.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, let me ask you: It speaks for itself, doesn't it? At least as far as a number of issues are concerned, but some issues that warrant a further clarification, if you ask me. Why are they making sure to preserve the casings, empty cartridges? Why would they need to do that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Empty cartridges can be used or re-used to produce new cartridges and new ammunition in the special-purpose production ammunition factories, be it in Republika Srpska or in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two references there: Prvi Partizan and Fasau from Uzice. Was that another company involved in a special-purpose production, and did it have the same status as Prvi Partizan?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Fasau enjoyed the same status. I'm not familiar with their production, really. I assume that they were the plant that was busy processing or reprocessing these raw materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document suggestions that a document was drawn up between Republika Srpska and these two companies. And now I'm asking you, Why is this addressed the to defence ministry, and how is the defence ministry involved in all of this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we are looking at here is the government or the defence ministry allocating to the Main Staff of the VRS certain funds, a certain amount of funds to be used for this purpose. And then the VRS Main Staff was manned to purchase ammunition in Yugoslavia. In order to be able to do that, they had to inform the defence ministry, made sure they knew about this business. Secondly, the defence ministry was in charge of issuing appropriate authorisations in order to make sure this could occur in a purely financial sense and in order to make sure the goods cleared the customs and police at the border, letting them know that the ammunition was rightfully purchased in the FRY and should be allowed to cross into another country's territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we be granted a number for this document, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D410. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leaving ammunition behind, let's move on to the issue of fuel that we have touched upon somewhat already. Your Honours, I would now have to address the Chamber. And the witness should perhaps leave the courtroom for a minute to address the procedural situation we are now confronted with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, counsel requests that you give us a minute. We'll call you just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to go through the statements and evidence of Mr. Djorde Djukic that was admitted under Rule 92 quater as OTP evidence and also some other Defence evidence pursuant to 92 quater. In keeping with your guide-lines, I would like to put to the witness some portions of Mr. Djukic's evidence without letting him know whose evidence this is. He wouldn't have anything on his screen whereas you would have the relevant evidence before you and would be able to follow the witness's answers. Mr. Djukic had given several statements that were admitted into evidence, and one of the topics involved is fuel. There is another topic that I would like to examine this witness on tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Am I to understand from counsel that these statements of General Djukic have not been shown to the witness in proofing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I showed him portions of the evidence without telling him who the author was. I merely asked him, Are you aware of this, did you know of this, and so on. I kept strictly to the guide-lines we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Give me just one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate in the proofing note references to this information, and I'm taking just a minute to make sure that I've received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why don't we proceed, Your Honour. I'm not successful in finding a reference to General Djukic. I want to make sure -- I may intervene at some point in time that this is beyond the scope of the proofing notes that I have received, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the list of documents I sent him, I informed Mr. Harmon that I would be using with this witness all the statements of Mr. Djukic's that were admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't dispute that at all, Your Honour. I'm just trying to see in the proofing note if there's reference to those statements, not that I haven't been referred to the statements, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't believe that I did include references in the proofing note. It was just another document that I used with the witness. And I informed Mr. Harmon of my intention to use the document with the witness. I didn't think it necessary to include in the proofing note what it was that the witness told me in response to this document. It was just a piece of evidence as any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to call your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest for Their Honours, while we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, to call up, for the benefit of Their Honours and, of course, not the witness himself, D397.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, how is it going to come up on our screens without coming up on his screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that we have already used this practice, so it's D397. And what I'd like to refer the witness to is on page 2 of 4 in B/C/S, and in English it's page 1 of 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do understand, though, that the transcript will stay in front of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the Chamber and the OTP, what I will be reading starts in the bottom: "There are continuous requests ..." If you can find it, Your Honours. This is the first portion I will read out for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I will be reading out to you a statement given by an individual, and I will ask you whether what you know on this issue that we are discussing now, which is fuel that was at the disposal of the VRS, whether what you remember of this issue is consistent with or not consistent with what I will read out for you. "There are continuous requests to the government for fuel, and every month requests are sent three or four times. Those requests are sent to the people in the directorate for commodity reserves. As far as I remember, around 40.000 tonnes of fuel and between 1.000 and 1.200 tonnes of kerosene were found in the reserves in Republika Srpska, so there were no problems regarding fuel provision until the beginning of 1995." Let me stop here. Based on the facts you know, is this an accurate representation of the situation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is accurate. And, in fact, I can state that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next portion I would like to refer you to is on the same page, Your Honours, the very bottom: [In English] "After one of those meetings, I talked to President Lukic" -- [Interpretation] Let me read you this. Let me read to you this: I talked to President Lukic, who told me that they had trading arrangements with the Croats and that he had met Jadranko Prlic regarding that issue. He said he hoped that, thanks to his talks with the Croats, there would be no problems with fuel."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then let's turn to the next page, a few lines down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "General Boric also told me that the meetings of the representatives of the Government of Republika Srpska and Croatian representatives were held in the village of Rujan, on the line of contact in the Bosansko Grahovo municipality. Apart from this, Boric told me that, in addition to president Lukic, the talks were attended by the minister of defence Dusan Kovacevic, minister of justice Jovo Rosic, and probably someone from the directorate for commodity reserves. I do not think that all the above-mentioned persons went to all the meetings. "Throughout this trade with Croats, as far as I know, 7.000 to 10.000 tonnes of fuel were procured, mostly diesel-2. The fuel was transported in tank trucks owned by private persons and companies from the area of Republika Srpska." General, do you agree with what is stated here? Are the facts as you know them consistent with what we have read out here about the procurement of fuel, let's call it that way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I was involved in these talks with representatives of Herceg Bosna led by Jadranko Prlic. It is true that we discussed other issues too, primarily the issue of a cease-fire along all the lines where the confronted parties were Croats and Serbs. It is also true that it was stated at this meeting that President Karadzic and Mate Boban had agreed that this meeting should take place and that we, and by "we" I mean both sides, were there on their orders. It is true that it was agreed there that the Army of Republika Srpska should turn over to the Croatian side -- should turn ammunition over to the Croatian side and that the Croatian side should, in turn, procure the VRS with fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was or who is Jadranko Prlic, I mean, what was his function at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the prime minister of Herceg Bosna, headquartered in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to read another portion, Your Honours, in the middle of this large paragraph: "I know that fuel was taken to split." If you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, please listen what I will read out. And then I will ask you for your comments. "I know that the the fuel was taken in Split. Our tank trucks went with civilian registration plates of Republika Srpska. There were usually around 15 tank trucks in each convoy so that a single convoy could transport 250 to 300 tonnes of fuel. There were no major problems during the transport except for slight traffic accidents. In this way, the fuel was delivered to Banja Luka into the commodity reserves warehouse and to Bileca and Bijeljina and some small quantities to Pale. The trade lasted around a year and a half, in the period from mid-1993 until the end of 1994." General, does what you remember of this tally with what I've read out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it does. But can I give you an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it that you disagree with something, or would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to explain how I came to know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quantity that was taken out of the general area of Split is something that I was familiar with. It was just under a hundred tank trucks. It was a very long convoy. This was the largest quantity of fuel ever to have been shipped in one convoy from the area of Split to the territory of Republika Srpska. It is correct - and I had information to that effect, although the information never came from official sources - that the Army of Republika Srpska often purchased fuel from the Croatian side. And most often that this happened locally, at local levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't want to go beyond our time, but I would like to just put one more question. And if we could go into private session for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. And once again, Mr. Kovacevic, just to remind you that we are now going to take a break until tomorrow morning at 9.00, and you are not supposed to discuss the case with anybody during the break until you are excused from testifying. The Court stands adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
